nameStory: The Humpback gets its common name from the distinctive slightly raised bump or hump in the center of its gray cap. This little fungal 'humpback whale' of the forest floor sports this characteristic umbonate shape that makes it easy to spot among the mosses where it grows.
description: The Humpback is a small to medium-sized mushroom with a gray cap that has a characteristic raised bump in the center. It typically grows 2-5 centimeters wide with distinctive forked gills that run down the stem. The entire mushroom has a whitish stem that can reach up to 8 centimeters tall, and the flesh may develop reddish stains when handled or cut.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Gray and slightly convex with a distinctive raised bump (umbo) in the center, feeling smooth to the touch and measuring 2-5 cm across

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Whitish gills that fork like tiny tree branches and run down the stem (decurrent), creating a distinctive pattern when viewed from below

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Whitish and can grow quite tall for the cap size, up to 8 cm, feeling firm and solid when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: White flesh may develop reddish stains when cut or bruised, appearing gradually over several minutes

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Mild, pleasant smell with no strong or unpleasant odors - often described as faintly mushroomy or earthy

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Produces a white spore print when cap is placed gill-side down on dark paper overnight

habitat: Look for Humpbacks in boggy, moist areas and under coniferous trees throughout New England's forests. They have a special relationship with mosses, particularly growing among Polytrichum moss and other moss species in wet, acidic soils. You'll often find them in the transition zones between wetlands and conifer stands.

seasonality.spring: Generally not active, as soil is still too cool and wet from snowmelt for fruiting.
seasonality.summer: Begins fruiting in mid to late summer, especially after periods of steady rain when mossy areas stay consistently moist.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for finding fresh specimens, continuing to fruit well into autumn until hard frosts arrive.
seasonality.winter: No active fruiting, though dried specimens may persist under snow cover.

funFact: The Humpback has formed a fascinating partnership with mosses - it actually helps create the perfect microhabitat for moss growth while the mosses provide it with nutrients, creating a tiny ecosystem you can observe in a space smaller than your dinner plate!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the False Chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca), which has similar forked gills but is bright orange instead of gray. Remember: 'Orange for caution, gray for the Humpback' - the color difference is your best clue.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name similarity to chanterelles and its forked gills, the Humpback is not closely related to true chanterelles and belongs to the waxcap family instead. This is a good example of how common names can be misleading about actual family relationships in fungi.
compareHints: The Humpback is the only species in its genus Cantharellula found in New England, making it unique among local fungi. Compared to other members of the waxcap family, it stands out with its gray coloration and strong association with mosses, while most other waxcaps are brightly colored and grow directly from soil.
